questions.question: The diagram shows a female human reproductive system. Where would the corpus luteum be found?
questions.answer: The corpus luteum forms from the remains of the follicle in the ovary after ovulation. B points to the ovary (A is the fallopian tube/uterine tube, C the uterus and D the cervix/vagina).
options: A
B
C
D

questions.question: In humans, active immunity includes:
questions.answer: Active immunity is part of the adaptive response, in which the body makes its own antibodies. Helper T cells activate B cells, which become plasma cells and memory cells (D). Antibodies are made by B cells (plasma cells), not T cells; physical barriers and inflammation are innate defences.
options: the production of antibodies by T cells.
prevention of infection with the use of physical barriers such as skin and mucous membranes.
activation of the inflammatory response.
activation of B cells by helper T cells.

questions.question: Two heterozygous parents are bred together to produce offspring. What percentage of the offspring would be heterozygous?
questions.answer: $Aa\times Aa$ gives $AA:Aa:aa$ in the ratio $1:2:1$, so $50\%$ are heterozygous (B).

questions.question: Which of the following correctly identifies a part of the human eye and its function?
questions.answer: The ciliary muscles change the shape of the lens (accommodation) so that light is focused on the retina (B). The image falls on the retina, not the optic nerve (A); the retina, not the sclera, detects light (C); the pupil controls how much light enters (D).
options: The lens focuses incoming light so that an image falls on the optic nerve.
The ciliary muscles contract or relax to modify the shape of the lens.
The sclera detects incoming light energy and converts it to an electrical potential.
The pupil protects the interior of the eye from damage from dust, scratches, or similar.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about proteins is true?
questions.answer: Structural proteins such as collagen and keratin support cells and tissues (C). Proteins are chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds; nitrogenous bases and phosphodiester bonds belong to nucleic acids, and RNA polymerase makes RNA (ribosomes make proteins).
options: Proteins are composed of long chains of nitrogenous bases.
Proteins contain phosphodiester bonds.
Proteins provide structure and support for cells.
Proteins are synthesized by RNA polymerase.

questions.question: Which of the following best identifies the reproductive methods available to the organisms listed?
questions.answer: Fungi reproduce asexually by budding (yeasts) or by spores (A). Plants also reproduce sexually, bacteria reproduce asexually (binary fission) and protists use several methods, not only spores, so B, C and D are incomplete or incorrect.
options: Fungi reproduce through budding or spores.
Plants reproduce through vegetative propagation.
Bacteria reproduce through sexual or asexual reproduction.
Protists reproduce through spores.

questions.question: The DNA that exists in prokaryotic cells is:
questions.answer: Prokaryotes have a single circular, double-stranded chromosome (plus plasmids) in the cytoplasm (B).
options: linear and double-stranded.
circular and double-stranded.
linear and single-stranded.
circular and single-stranded.

questions.question: Colour-blindness is an inherited disease. The Punnett square shows the F1 generation of offspring of a woman who is colour blind and a man with unaffected vision. Which of the following conclusions can be drawn from the Punnett square?
questions.answer: The mother is $X^bX^b$ and the father is $X^BY$. All daughters are $X^BX^b$ (unaffected carriers) and all sons are $X^bY$ (colour blind). So female offspring have a $100\%$ chance of being carriers (C). Males have a $100\%$ (not $50\%$) chance of being colour blind, and the trait is recessive.
options: Any male offspring have a 50% chance of being colour blind.
Colour-blindness is a dominant trait.
Any female offspring have a 100% chance of being carriers for the condition.
Any female offspring have a 100% chance of being colour blind.

questions.question: In 1970, the most common type of corn grown in the USA was a variety known as TCMS corn. Around this time, the rapid spread of the fungus *Bipolaris maydis* led to almost 100% of corn crops in some states being wiped out. The economic losses totalled approximately 1 billion USD. Farmers attempting to recover from the disaster found that other corn varieties were able to be cultivated in previously infected fields. The most significant biological factor contributing to the disaster was probably:
questions.answer: Almost all corn grown was a single, genetically uniform variety, so all plants were susceptible to the same fungus. Other varieties grew in the infected fields, showing that genetic diversity gives resilience. The key factor was a lack of biodiversity (C).
options: genetic drift.
artificial pollination.
a lack of biodiversity.
gene cloning.

questions.question: Which cells are likely to be found in abundance in the lymph nodes?
questions.answer: Lymph nodes filter lymph and contain large numbers of white blood cells, including macrophages, B cells and T cells (C).
options: Muscle cells
Red blood cells
Macrophages
Neurons

questions.question: Which of the following describes a physiological adaptation to regulate internal body temperature?
questions.answer: Vasodilation of skin blood vessels, which increases heat loss, is an internal body process, so it is a physiological adaptation (C). Licking and huddling are behavioural adaptations, and a layer of fat is a structural adaptation.
options: A kangaroo licks its paws to stimulate evaporative cooling.
Fairy penguin chicks huddle in a group to conserve body heat.
Blood vessels close to the skin dilate in hot temperatures.
Polar bears possess thick layers of insulating fat.

questions.question: The following poster was used as part of a breast cancer awareness campaign. What is the most effective way to assess the impact of this campaign?
questions.answer: The campaign urges women to get screened for early detection, so the most direct measure of its effect is the change in the number of women screened (B). Incidence and mortality change slowly and are affected by many other factors; attitudes do not show changed behaviour.
options: Compare data on the incidence of breast cancer before and after the campaign.
Compare the number of women being screened for breast cancer before and after the campaign.
Survey women in the population to find out their attitudes towards breast cancer.
Compare the mortality rate of women before and after the campaign.

questions.question: What is the difference between co-dominance and incomplete dominance?
questions.answer: In co-dominance both alleles are fully expressed in the heterozygote (e.g. red and white patches). In incomplete dominance the heterozygote shows a blend (e.g. pink), so neither parental trait appears fully (A).
options: Co-dominance: both traits appear in the phenotype. Incomplete dominance: neither trait appears in the phenotype.
Co-dominance: the dominant allele partially masks the recessive allele. Incomplete dominance: neither allele blocks the expression of the other allele.
Co-dominance: an intermediate phenotype occurs. Incomplete dominance: an alternating phenotype occurs.
Co-dominance: neither trait appears in the phenotype. Incomplete dominance: both traits appear in the phenotype.

questions.question: *Echeveria elegans* is a species of succulent whose leaves are coated with a wax which makes the plant's fleshy leaves appear to gleam in the sun. Which of the following best explains how this wax coating helps the plants to maintain water balance?
questions.answer: The pale wax reflects sunlight, reducing heating and so water loss by evaporation and transpiration (D).
options: It increases transpiration from the leaves.
It increases the water absorbed by the plant.
It causes rain water to pool on the leaves.
It reflects sunlight.

questions.question: Some students were removing the epithelium from a leaf as part of a school experiment. One student spilled sap from inside the leaf onto their hand, which resulted in redness and swelling. What mechanism in the plant could explain the development of the rash?
questions.answer: Plants have no adaptive immune system, no blood vessels to dilate and no inflammatory response. The irritating chemicals in the sap are part of the plant's innate chemical defences against herbivores and pathogens (D). The redness and swelling occur in the student (an inflammatory response), not in the plant.
options: Adaptive immunity
Vasodilation
Inflammation
Innate immunity

questions.question: Identify the INCORRECT statement from the list below.
questions.answer: Intracellular pathogens replicate inside host cells; it is extracellular pathogens that live in the interstitial fluid. Statement B is incorrect. The other three statements are correct.
options: PAMPs stands for pathogen-associated molecular patterns
Intracellular pathogens replicate in the interstitial fluid that bathes tissues
The innate and adaptive immune responses can occur simultaneously
Inflammation and phagocytosis are two elements of the innate immune response

questions.question: Tahlia was vaccinated against measles just after her son Alex's birth. Specific antibodies that attack measles are transferred to Alex via Tahlia's breastmilk. When exposed to the measles virus, these antibodies prevent Alex from becoming ill. Which type of human defence to disease is responsible for Alex's immunity to measles?
questions.answer: Specific antibodies are produced by the adaptive response (Tahlia's B cells), and Alex receives them as passive immunity. Of the options, only the adaptive immune response involves specific antibodies (D).
options: Physical barrier
Chemical barrier
Innate immune response
Adaptive immune response

questions.question: The following information refers to three different non-infectious diseases. Duchenne muscular dystrophy is a rare X-linked condition characterised by progressive muscular degeneration and weakness. Keshan disease is a reversible form of congestive heart failure. It is caused by a lack of the element selenium in the body. Arsenicosis is a condition that occurs due to exposure to high levels of arsenic. It can occur in people whose workplaces, homes or groundwater have been contaminated with industrial arsenic. Which of the following shows the correct classification of these diseases?
questions.answer: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is inherited (genetic). Keshan disease is caused by a dietary deficiency of selenium (nutritional). Arsenicosis is caused by exposure to arsenic in the environment (environmental) (B).
options: Duchenne: Nutritional; Keshan: Environmental; Arsenicosis: Genetic
Duchenne: Genetic; Keshan: Nutritional; Arsenicosis: Environmental
Duchenne: Genetic; Keshan: Environmental; Arsenicosis: Environmental
Duchenne: Environmental; Keshan: Genetic; Arsenicosis: Nutritional

questions.question: The diagram shows a process that occurs during cell division. Which of the following is correct?
questions.answer: The diagram shows homologous chromosomes pairing and exchanging segments (crossing over), which occurs in prophase I of meiosis. This produces new combinations of existing alleles, increasing the variety of possible genotypes. It does not create new alleles (that requires mutation) (B).
options: Type of division: Meiosis; outcome for offspring: greater variety of possible alleles
Type of division: Meiosis; outcome for offspring: greater variety of possible genotypes
Type of division: Mitosis; outcome for offspring: greater variety of possible alleles
Type of division: Mitosis; outcome for offspring: greater variety of possible genotypes

questions.question: The graph shows the changing concentration of an antibody in a patient's blood. Which of the below correctly accounts for a component of the graph?
questions.answer: The second, larger and faster peak is the secondary response. Memory B cells formed during the first exposure rapidly proliferate and differentiate into plasma cells that secrete large amounts of antibody (D).
options: T-cell activity is stimulated by inoculation with a vaccine.
Passive immunity occurs more slowly than active immunity.
Antigen-presenting cells exist in higher concentrations following secondary exposure to a pathogen.
Existing memory B-cells rapidly proliferate to produce plasma cells.

questions.question: The possession of one of two types of earlobes (hanging or attached) is sometimes used to study the inheritance of characteristics in humans. The pedigree shows the different types of earlobes present in three generations. Identify the pattern of inheritance shown in the pedigree and justify your answer.
questions.answer:
**Autosomal recessive.**
- Two unaffected (hanging earlobe) parents, II-2 and II-3, have an affected child, III-1, so the trait must be recessive and both parents are carriers.
- It is not X-linked recessive: the affected mother I-4 has unaffected sons (II-3 and II-4), but under X-linked recessive inheritance all of an affected mother's sons would be affected.

questions.question: The pedigree shows the different types of earlobes present in three generations (hanging earlobes dominant; attached earlobes recessive). Identify the genotype of III-1 (a female with attached earlobes).
questions.answer: III-1 shows the recessive trait, so she is homozygous recessive, e.g. $ee$.

questions.question: Hearing disorders occur when the normal function of the ear is disrupted or impaired. Name ONE hearing disorder and describe how the normal function of the ear is disrupted or impaired in this scenario.
questions.answer: **Sensorineural hearing loss.** Normally, sound vibrations pass through the middle ear to the cochlea, where hair cells convert them into nerve impulses that the auditory nerve carries to the brain. In sensorineural hearing loss the hair cells in the cochlea (or the auditory nerve) are damaged, so vibrations are not converted into electrical signals and transmitted, and the brain cannot interpret sound (especially faint and high-pitched sounds).

questions.question: Hearing disorders occur when the normal function of the ear is disrupted or impaired. Suggest a suitable technology to assist people living with sensorineural hearing loss and justify its use.
questions.answer: A **cochlear implant**. A microphone picks up sound, a speech processor converts it into electrical signals, and an electrode array in the cochlea stimulates the auditory nerve directly. This is suitable because in sensorineural hearing loss the hair cells are damaged and cannot transform sound vibrations into nerve impulses, so the implant bypasses the damaged part. (Hearing aids, which only amplify sound, suit mild loss where some inner-ear function remains.)

questions.question: Two students choose different activities to complete over 15 minutes. Student A eats an ice cream while Student B goes for a run. Afterwards, the students wondered how the two activities would affect their blood glucose levels. Draw a labelled flow chart or diagram to show the changes that take place in both Student A and Student B in response to their activities, including any changes in hormone levels and the role of named internal organs.
questions.answer:
**Student A (ice cream):** blood glucose rises $\to$ detected by the pancreas, where beta cells release **insulin** (insulin level rises) $\to$ body cells take up more glucose and the **liver** converts glucose to glycogen for storage $\to$ blood glucose falls back to the normal level.

**Student B (run):** respiration in muscles uses glucose, so blood glucose falls $\to$ detected by the pancreas, where alpha cells release **glucagon** (glucagon level rises, insulin falls) $\to$ the **liver** breaks down glycogen to glucose and releases it into the blood $\to$ blood glucose rises back to the normal level.

Both are negative feedback loops that restore blood glucose to its normal range. (School's flow chart is shown.)

questions.question: Coat colour in rabbits is a monogenic trait controlled by multiple alleles. The wild-type allele, $B$, is expressed as brown fur. The chinchilla allele, $b^{ch}$, is expressed as black-tipped white fur. The Himalayan allele, $b^h$, is expressed as black fur on the ears, feet and nose, with white fur elsewhere. Finally, the albino allele, $b$, is expressed as white fur. Brown fur is dominant over the chinchilla, Himalayan and albino fur colours. Chinchilla is incompletely dominant over Himalayan and albino, and Himalayan is dominant over albino. Explain how it is possible for two brown rabbits to produce albino offspring.
questions.answer: Both brown parents can be heterozygous, $Bb\times Bb$, each carrying one recessive albino allele $b$. There is a $25\%$ chance ($1$ in $4$) that an offspring inherits $b$ from both parents (genotype $bb$), which is expressed as albino.

questions.question: Coat colour in rabbits is controlled by multiple alleles: $B$ (brown), $b^{ch}$ (chinchilla), $b^h$ (Himalayan) and $b$ (albino). Chinchilla is incompletely dominant over Himalayan and albino, and Himalayan is dominant over albino. A heterozygous Himalayan rabbit was crossed with a chinchilla rabbit. Use a Punnett square to determine the possible genotypes of the offspring and calculate the percentage of the offspring that can be expected to possess each genotype.
questions.answer:
Heterozygous Himalayan: $b^hb$. Chinchilla: $b^{ch}b^{ch}$.

| | $b^h$ | $b$ |
|---|---|---|
| $b^{ch}$ | $b^{ch}b^h$ | $b^{ch}b$ |
| $b^{ch}$ | $b^{ch}b^h$ | $b^{ch}b$ |

$50\%$ $b^{ch}b^h$ and $50\%$ $b^{ch}b$.

questions.question: Coat colour in rabbits is controlled by multiple alleles. Chinchilla ($b^{ch}$, black-tipped white fur) is incompletely dominant over Himalayan ($b^h$) and albino ($b$). A breeder found that a chinchilla rabbit from his stock gave birth to a baby rabbit with light grey fur. Suggest how this might have occurred and justify your answer.
questions.answer: The chinchilla rabbit was crossed with a Himalayan (or albino) rabbit, giving an offspring of genotype $b^{ch}b^h$ (or $b^{ch}b$). Because chinchilla is incompletely dominant over Himalayan and albino, the heterozygote shows a blended phenotype, which would be light grey (between black-tipped white and white/Himalayan).

questions.question: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency (G6PDD) is a genetic disorder that occurs almost exclusively in males (X-linked recessive). Cindy has a brother called Dominic who is affected by G6PDD, as well as another brother, Harry, who is not affected. Their sister, Jillian, has had genetic testing completed and knows that she does not possess an affected allele. Cindy's father, Jack, is not affected but her mother, Fiona, is a carrier of the condition. State the genotypes for Dominic, Harry, Jillian and Fiona.
questions.answer:
Let $X^d$ be the G6PDD allele.
- Dominic (affected): $X^dY$
- Harry (unaffected): $XY$
- Jillian (no affected allele): $XX$
- Fiona (carrier): $X^dX$

questions.question: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency (G6PDD) is a genetic disorder that occurs almost exclusively in males. Raymond comes from a family that has no record of G6PDD. Raymond is married to Cindy. Cindy has a brother called Dominic who is affected by G6PDD, as well as another brother, Harry, who is not affected by the condition. Their sister, Jillian, does not possess an affected allele. Cindy's father, Jack, is not affected but her mother, Fiona, is a carrier. Raymond and Cindy have recently had a son who they named Victor. Construct a pedigree to show the occurrence of G6PDD in the family. Include a key.
questions.answer: Jack (unaffected male square) and Fiona (carrier female, half-shaded circle) are the parents of Dominic (affected male, shaded square), Harry (unaffected male), Cindy (female, status unknown, '?') and Jillian (unaffected female). Cindy is married to Raymond (unaffected male), and their son Victor has unknown status ('?'). The key identifies carrier female, unaffected female, unaffected male and affected male. (School's pedigree shown.)

questions.question: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency (G6PDD) is X-linked recessive. Cindy's mother Fiona is a carrier and her father Jack is unaffected. Raymond comes from a family with no record of G6PDD. Raymond and Cindy have recently had a son named Victor. Analyse the likelihood that Victor will be affected by G6PDD.
questions.answer:
Cindy received an X chromosome from each parent. Jack gave her his unaffected $X$, while Fiona ($X^dX$) gave either $X^d$ or $X$, so there is a $50\%$ chance that Cindy is a carrier.
- If Cindy is a carrier ($X^dX$), she passes $X^d$ to a son with probability $50\%$. Raymond ($XY$) provides the $Y$, so Victor would have a $50\%$ chance of being affected.
- If Cindy is not a carrier ($XX$), Victor cannot inherit the allele, so the chance is $0\%$.

Overall the likelihood is $50\%\times50\%=25\%$ that Victor is affected.

questions.question:
A sequence of DNA from the template strand of a particular gene is shown below.

TAC GGA TCT **AGA ATA AAA** CGG AAT GCT GGG **ACA CGG** GTA ACT

The highlighted (bold) sections of DNA are introns. What do the other sections represent?
questions.answer: Exons (the coding sections that remain in the mature mRNA).

questions.question:
A sequence of DNA from the template strand of a particular gene is shown below.

TAC GGA TCT **AGA ATA AAA** CGG AAT GCT GGG **ACA CGG** GTA ACT

The bold sections are introns. Determine the sequence of the mature mRNA that would be produced from the above gene.
questions.answer:
Remove the introns, leaving the template exons TAC GGA TCT CGG AAT GCT GGG GTA ACT. mRNA is complementary (A pairs with U):
**AUG CCU AGA GCC UUA CGA CCC CAU UGA**

questions.question: The mature mRNA from a gene is AUG CCU AGA GCC UUA CGA CCC CAU UGA. Using the mRNA codon table, state the sequence of amino acids that would be produced.
questions.answer:
AUG = Met, CCU = Pro, AGA = Arg, GCC = Ala, UUA = Leu, CGA = Arg, CCC = Pro, CAU = His, UGA = stop.
**Met – Pro – Arg – Ala – Leu – Arg – Pro – His** (the stop codon does not code for an amino acid).

questions.question: The diagram shows the levels of pituitary and ovarian hormones present in the blood at different stages of the menstrual cycle. At what approximate day of the reproductive cycle does ovulation occur?
questions.answer: Day $14$ (day $13$ was also accepted), at the LH peak.

questions.question: The diagram shows the levels of pituitary and ovarian hormones present in the blood at different stages of the menstrual cycle. Explain the role of ONE hormone in bringing about ovulation. Include reference to the shape of the graph.
questions.answer: **Luteinising hormone (LH).** The graph shows a sharp peak in LH at about day $13$–$14$, just before ovulation. This surge in LH triggers the rupture of the mature follicle and the release of the egg (ovulation), and then the follicle develops into the corpus luteum.

questions.question: If an egg is fertilised following ovulation, high progesterone and oestrogen levels must be maintained in order to sustain a pregnancy. Describe how these high levels are achieved with reference to TWO named structures.
questions.answer: The **corpus luteum** (the remains of the follicle) continues to secrete progesterone and oestrogen in early pregnancy, stimulated by hCG released by the embryo, so the endometrium is maintained. Later the **placenta** develops and takes over secretion of high levels of progesterone and oestrogen, and the corpus luteum breaks down. (Oestrogen also comes from the ovaries before and during this time.)

questions.question: During labour, contractions of the uterus cause the posterior pituitary gland to release oxytocin. Oxytocin stimulates more uterine and muscle contractions to push the baby through the birth canal. Explain why this mechanism is considered an example of a positive feedback loop.
questions.answer: In a positive feedback loop the response strengthens (amplifies) the original stimulus. Uterine contractions stimulate the release of oxytocin, and oxytocin causes stronger and more frequent contractions, which stimulate even more oxytocin release, until the baby is delivered.

questions.question: The diagram shows the process of phagocytosis. Chediak-Higashi Syndrome is a rare inherited disorder of the immune system in which the proteins that regulate the formation of a phagolysosome are defective. Explain why this would negatively impact both the innate immune response and the adaptive immune response.
questions.answer:
**Innate:** if phagolysosomes cannot form, the lysosomal enzymes cannot digest ingested microbes, so phagocytes such as macrophages and neutrophils cannot destroy pathogens. This non-specific defence is severely limited, leaving only responses that do not need phagocytosis, such as inflammation and complement proteins.

**Adaptive:** digesting pathogens is needed so that antigen-presenting cells can display pathogen antigens on their surface. Without this antigen presentation, the clonal selection and proliferation of the specific helper T cells and B cells would be delayed or reduced, so the adaptive response is weaker.

questions.question: The graph depicts cases of Ebola Virus Disease measured during an outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo between 2018–2019. The WHO's strategy focused on: (1) detection and rapid isolation of cases; (2) intensification of rapid multidisciplinary public health actions around any confirmed case; (3) strengthening community engagement; (4) strengthening the health system and coordination of local and international partners. Public health officials struggled to implement these measures early in the outbreak due to difficulty accessing remote areas, socio-political unrest and armed conflict. Evaluate the effectiveness of the public health measures used to control the outbreak.
questions.answer: The measures were not effective at first but became effective. From the graph, weekly cases kept rising through late 2018 and early 2019, reaching a peak of about $130$ cases per week in April 2019, and the cumulative total rose steeply to roughly $2000$ cases by mid-2019. This reflects the difficulties of access and unrest. After the peak, as the measures were successfully implemented, weekly cases fell steadily to near zero by November 2019 and the cumulative curve flattened at about $3300$ cases, which shows the outbreak was being brought under control. The strategy was therefore effective overall, though delayed, and many cases occurred before it took hold.

questions.question: The WHO's measures to control an Ebola outbreak were: (1) detection and rapid isolation of cases; (2) intensification of rapid multidisciplinary public health actions around any confirmed case; (3) strengthening community engagement; (4) strengthening the health system and effective coordination of local and international partners. Explain how any TWO of these measures may have contributed to controlling the outbreak.
questions.answer:
**Detection and rapid isolation of cases:** isolating infectious people quickly reduces the time they spend in the community, so there are fewer opportunities for the virus to be transmitted from one person to another, which reduces the number of new cases and the spread.

**Strengthening community engagement:** when the community understands the disease and trusts health workers, more people cooperate with measures such as reporting symptoms, safe burials and isolation, so a larger proportion of the population takes precautions that limit transmission, making the other measures more effective at a population level.

questions.question: Describe the process of DNA replication with reference to the roles of at least TWO named enzymes.
questions.answer: DNA replication is semi-conservative and occurs in the nucleus before cell division. **Helicase** unwinds and unzips the double helix by breaking the hydrogen bonds between bases, forming a replication fork. **Primase** adds short RNA primers. **DNA polymerase** then adds complementary nucleotides to each template strand in the $5'\to3'$ direction (continuously on the leading strand, and in Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand) and replaces the primers with DNA. **Ligase** joins the fragments together. The result is two identical DNA molecules, each with one original and one new strand.

questions.question: Evaluate the impact of scientific knowledge on the manipulation of plant and animal reproduction in agriculture.
questions.answer:
Understanding of inheritance and of reproductive mechanisms has allowed farmers to control which organisms reproduce, increasing yield, quality and uniformity.

**Plants:** knowledge of pollination led to artificial pollination (dusting pollen from a chosen plant onto the stigma of another) and hybridisation, e.g. Federation wheat combining disease and drought resistance with high grain quality. Knowledge of vegetative propagation allows cloning, e.g. banana plants from cuttings or tissue culture, producing genetically identical plants with desired traits.

**Animals:** selective breeding of parents with desired traits has produced Belgian Blue cattle with high lean-beef yields and Jersey–Friesian crosses with high-quality milk. Artificial insemination lets semen from a selected male be used over long distances with lower risk of disease or injury, and embryo transfer lets many offspring be produced from elite females.

**Evaluation:** this knowledge has greatly improved productivity and the predictability of traits, so manipulation is now faster and more precise than natural breeding. The cost is reduced genetic diversity (which makes crops and herds vulnerable to disease), but overall the impact on agricultural production has been large and positive.

questions.question: The diagram represents the life cycle for an enveloped RNA virus. The host cell depicted is a human cell. Describe the process shown to occur at stage 4.
questions.answer: Stage 4 is **translation**. A ribosome reads the viral mRNA in groups of three bases (codons), beginning at a start codon. Each codon is matched by a complementary anticodon on a tRNA, and each tRNA carries a specific amino acid. The ribosome forms peptide bonds between adjacent amino acids, and the polypeptide grows codon by codon until a stop codon is reached, producing viral proteins.

questions.question: The diagram represents the life cycle for an enveloped RNA virus in a human host cell. Stage 4 is translation of viral mRNA. Assess the importance of this process to the virus.
questions.answer: It is vital for virus replication, because translation produces the viral proteins (including the envelope and coat proteins and the enzymes) that are needed to assemble new copies of the virus. Without it, no new virus particles could be produced, because viruses depend on the host cell's ribosomes and cannot make proteins themselves.

questions.question: An infected person received a vaccination several months earlier containing the modified antigen shown (an inactive particle with the same outer features as the enveloped virus). The infected person experienced only minor symptoms and recovered more quickly than expected. Using your understanding of the human immune system, explain why this occurred.
questions.answer:
The modified antigen has the same external features (envelope proteins) as the virus but lacks the viral RNA, so it cannot replicate but is recognised by the immune system.

**Primary response (vaccination):** antigen-presenting cells display fragments of the antigen to helper T cells, which activate B cells and cytotoxic T cells through clonal selection. B cells proliferate into plasma cells that make antibodies, and memory B and T cells are formed and persist after the antigen is cleared.

**Secondary response (infection):** when the person is infected with the real virus, which has the same antigens, memory cells recognise it and respond faster and more strongly. Memory B cells rapidly proliferate to produce many plasma cells, so antibody concentration rises sooner and reaches a higher peak than in a primary response, and memory T cells quickly destroy infected cells. The virus is cleared before it can multiply extensively, which is why the person had only minor symptoms and recovered quickly.
